title: Commands, events and logs
summary: What you send (command, event, query) decides the channel (queue, publish-subscribe, log), and every choice has a cost you must design for.

steps.title: Commands, events and queries
body: Three kinds of message, three different contracts:
| | **Command** | **Event** | **Query** |
| Name | `PlaceOrder`, `SendInvoice` (imperative) | `OrderPlaced`, `PaymentDeclined` (past tense) | `GetOrderStatus` |
| Receivers | exactly **one** owner | zero to many, unknown to the publisher | one, and the caller waits |
| Can it be refused? | yes, the owner may reject it | no, it already happened | n/a |
| Natural channel | a queue (point-to-point) | publish-subscribe or a log | usually a sync call (HTTP, gRPC) |
Why it matters: an event named like a command (`SendWelcomeEmail` broadcast to everyone) means the publisher
decides what others do, which is coupling dressed up as messaging. Publish the **fact** (`CustomerRegistered`)
and let each subscriber decide.
A query over messaging is request-reply: a `ReplyTo` queue and a `CorrelationId` to match the answer. It works,
but if you need the answer now a direct call is usually simpler.

steps.explain: Imperative names ask one owner to do something; past-tense names announce a fact; questions want an answer back.

steps.title: Three channel shapes
body: ```text
Point-to-point queue (destructive read)
producer ──> [ m3 m2 m1 ] ──> worker-1      m1 is gone once worker-1 acks it
└──> worker-2      workers compete: each message goes to one of them
Publish-subscribe (a copy per subscription)
producer ──> exchange / topic ──> [ billing queue ] ──> billing
└──> [ email queue   ] ──> email
a subscriber that binds later only sees messages published after it bound
Append-only log (replayable, offsets)
billing at 3    email at 6 (caught up)
In a **log** (Kafka, RabbitMQ streams, Event Hubs, Kinesis) reading does **not** delete. Each consumer group
keeps its own committed **offset**; records go away only by retention (time or size) or compaction. Replay is
just moving an offset back, and a brand-new group can start from the beginning.
> **See it:** open **Labs → Messaging builder → RabbitMQ** and play *Everyone gets a copy*, then switch to
> **Kafka** and play *The new service saw nothing*.

steps.prompt: Two consumer groups read the same log. What does this print?
code: Console.WriteLine($"{group}: lag {log.Count - offset}, next {(offset < log.Count ? log[offset] : "-")}");
steps.explain: The offset is the position of the *next* record to read. Lag is the log-end offset minus the committed offset, exactly the LAG column of `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe`.

steps.prompt: A new fraud-scoring service must score the **last 7 days** of orders, then every new one. Billing already consumes the order events. What design works?
options: Orders on a Kafka topic with retention of at least 7 days; fraud uses its **own** consumer group with `AutoOffsetReset = Earliest`
Fraud consumes from the same RabbitMQ queue as billing
Bind a new RabbitMQ queue for fraud to the orders exchange
Ask the billing team to re-publish last week's orders
explain: Sharing billing's queue makes fraud and billing **compete**: each order goes to one of them. A newly bound
queue only receives messages published from now on. Only a log that kept the records can be replayed, and a
new group starts wherever `auto.offset.reset` says when it has no committed offset.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: looking at a broker
steps.body: The first five minutes of any messaging incident are spent looking, so reach for these to see where the messages are, who reads them and how far behind each group is (try them in **Labs → Live network labs → 24 Live RabbitMQ lab** and **25 Live Kafka lab**).

toolkit.cmd: rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged consumers
toolkit.what: RabbitMQ: where are the messages, and who is reading them?
flags: waiting for a consumer; growing means consumers are too slow or gone
delivered but not acked; high means consumers are stuck or prefetch is too big
how many consumers are attached to the queue

toolkit.what: Every consumer per queue, with its prefetch and whether it acks.
flags: how many unacked messages the consumer may hold

toolkit.what: Which exchange routes to which queue, with which routing key.
The same queue numbers from the management HTTP API, for scripts and dashboards.
flags: pick one number out of the JSON

toolkit.what: Kafka: how far behind is each group, partition by partition?
flags: CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG per partition
toolkit.when: LAG growing on every partition: the group is falling behind. On one partition only: a hot key or a stuck consumer.

toolkit.what: Where is the end of the log, per partition?
How the topic is laid out: partitions, leaders, replicas and in-sync replicas.
RabbitMQ prefetch: the first setting you reach for on a consumer.
flags: how many unacked messages one consumer may hold

toolkit.what: RabbitMQ publisher confirms: the broker tells the publisher it stored the message.
flags: turn confirms on for the channel

toolkit.cmd: new ProducerConfig { Acks = Acks.All, EnableIdempotence = true }
toolkit.what: Kafka producer settings you reach for first.
flags: the write counts only once the in-sync replicas have it

toolkit.cmd: new ConsumerConfig { AutoOffsetReset = AutoOffsetReset.Earliest, EnableAutoOffsetStore = false }
toolkit.what: Kafka consumer settings you reach for first.
flags: where a group with no committed offset starts
manual offset storing: you call StoreOffset after the work

steps.prompt: Match what you see to what it usually means.
pairs: Consumers are too slow or gone
Consumers are stuck or prefetch is too big
A hot key or a stuck consumer
steps.explain: Look before you touch anything: these four readings point you at the consumer, the prefetch, the group or one key.

steps.prompt: Which question does each command answer?
buckets: How is it wired or laid out?
steps.explain: Counts and lag tell you how much is waiting; `list_consumers` tells you who reads and with what prefetch; bindings and the topic layout tell you how messages get where they go.

steps.prompt: Match each cloud service to its shape.
pairs: A queue: one consumer gets each message, visibility timeout, redrive to a DLQ
Fan-out: one publish, a copy to every subscribed queue or endpoint
Publish-subscribe with named subscriptions, sessions and a built-in DLQ
A partitioned log with consumer groups and checkpoints (Kafka-compatible endpoint)
Publish-subscribe with ack deadlines, ordering keys and dead-letter topics
steps.explain: The names change between clouds, the three shapes do not. Map a new service onto queue, pub-sub or log first, then learn its limits.

steps.title: What messaging costs you
body: Messaging is not free. You trade a loud, immediate failure for quieter ones you must design for:
- **Eventual consistency.** The user sees "order placed", refreshes the order page, and it is not there yet.
Design the UI and the read side for "a moment later".
- **Duplicates.** Brokers deliver *at least once*: a crash between processing and ack redelivers. Every
consumer must be idempotent (module 4).
- **Ordering.** Only per queue or per partition, and competing consumers or retries reorder even that.
- **Operations.** One more stateful, clustered system: disks, upgrades, quorum, monitoring of depth, lag and
dead letters, and someone on call for it.
- **Debugging.** One request is now several hops in time. Carry a correlation id and the W3C `traceparent` in
message headers, or you will not be able to follow an order through the system.
Keep a **query** that needs an answer now synchronous. Use messaging where time or rate decoupling earns this bill.

steps.prompt: You replace the synchronous email call with an `OrderPlaced` event. Which **new** problems do you now have to handle? Select all that apply.
options: The same email can be sent twice after a consumer crash
Emails can lag behind orders during a spike
You need monitoring for queue depth and dead letters
Checkout fails whenever the email service is down
Emails may be sent in a different order than the orders were placed
explain: Checkout failing with the email service is the problem you just removed. In exchange you get at-least-once
duplicates, delay, ordering only per queue, and one more system to watch.

steps.title: Queues destroy, fan-out copies
prompt: Write a class `FanoutBroker` that models a fanout exchange with destructive queues:
- `void Bind(string queue)`: creates the queue (if new) and binds it; binding twice does nothing more.
- `void Publish(string message)`: puts a copy of the message into **every queue bound so far**.
- `string? Get(string queue)`: removes and returns the oldest message of that queue, or `null` if the queue is
A queue bound after a publish does **not** receive that message: that is the difference from a log.
solution: queues.TryGetValue(queue, out var q) && q.Count > 0 ? q.Dequeue() : null;
hints: A `Dictionary<string, Queue<string>>` from queue name to its messages.
`Publish` enqueues into every value; `Get` dequeues if there is something.
template: Dojo.Eq("email gets its own copy of A1", "A1", dojoF.Get("email"));
Dojo.Eq("reading removes: billing is empty", (string?)null, dojoF.Get("billing"));
Dojo.Eq("a late queue misses A1", "A2", dojoF.Get("fraud"));
Dojo.Eq("binding twice does not duplicate", "A2", dojoF.Get("email"));

steps.title: An append-only log with consumer groups
prompt: Now the other shape. Write a class `EventLog`:
- `long Append(string value)`: appends and returns the record's offset (`0`, `1`, `2`, ...).
- `long EndOffset`: the offset the **next** record will get (the log-end offset).
- `void Join(string group, bool fromEarliest)`: a new group starts at `0` when `fromEarliest`, else at
`EndOffset` (that is `auto.offset.reset`). Joining an existing group changes nothing.
- `List<string> Poll(string group, int max)`: returns up to `max` records from the group's position and moves
the position past them (as if committed). A group that never joined throws `InvalidOperationException`.
- `long Lag(string group)`: `EndOffset` minus the group's position.
- `void Seek(string group, long offset)`: moves the group's position (replay or skip). An offset below `0` or
Reading never removes anything: two groups read the same records independently.
starter: public void Join(string group, bool fromEarliest) { }
public List<string> Poll(string group, int max) => new();
public void Seek(string group, long offset) { }
solution: public void Join(string group, bool fromEarliest)
public List<string> Poll(string group, int max)
public long Lag(string group) => EndOffset - Position(group);
public void Seek(string group, long offset)
positions.TryGetValue(group, out var p) ? p : throw new InvalidOperationException($"group '{group}' has not joined");
hints: Keep a `List<string>` of records and a `Dictionary<string, long>` of positions per group.
`Poll`: `records.Skip((int)pos).Take(max).ToList()`, then advance the position by the count.
template: Dojo.Eq("end offset is the next offset", 3L, dojoLog.EndOffset);
Dojo.Eq("billing polls two", new List<string> { "A1", "A2" }, dojoLog.Poll("billing", 2));
Dojo.Eq("latest: a new group sees nothing old", new List<string>(), dojoLog.Poll("email", 10));
Dojo.Eq("email gets only the new record", new List<string> { "A4" }, dojoLog.Poll("email", 10));
Dojo.Eq("billing still reads independently", new List<string> { "A3", "A4" }, dojoLog.Poll("billing", 10));
Dojo.Eq("joining again does not reset", 0L, dojoLog.Lag("billing"));
Dojo.Eq("seek back replays", new List<string> { "A2", "A3" }, dojoLog.Poll("billing", 2));
